rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named Ḥā Mīm, like other sūrahs in this group, whose topics share common ground.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ānic name of this sūrah too is Ḥā Mīm.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The introduction resembles the preceding sūrah’s opening but describes a different aspect of the Qur’ān’s significance.
rows.anchor: Like the introductory part of the previous sūrah, this sūrah too contains a reference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanzīl conveys gradual progression and elaborate effort, expressing God’s thoroughness in revealing the Qur’ān.
rows.anchor: contains the meaning of gradual progression and elaborate effort

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAzīz means powerful and dominant, while al-Ḥakīm describes one whose every word and deed is wise.
rows.anchor: The former means powerful and dominant and the latter refers to someone whose each and every word and deed has some wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation is a royal decree from the universe’s sovereign Master and must be obeyed; no one can prevent His seizure if it is dishonoured.
rows.anchor: it is a royal decree of the real Master of this Universe Who must necessarily be obeyed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wisdom explains His continued respite: people may reform, while the truth is conclusively conveyed to those who waste their abilities.
rows.anchor: He keeps on extending their respite so that those who have the ability can mend their ways and make themselves worthy of His mercy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs supporting the Qur’ān’s call to monotheism and warning of judgement fill the world, but benefit only believers.
rows.anchor: they are useful only for those who profess faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who demand signs remain blind; even a newly shown sign would lead them to demand another.
rows.anchor: Those who do not profess faith remain blind even after observing everything and keep demanding more signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person’s intent is decisive: one seeking truth finds guidance throughout the heavens and earth, while desire obscures it.
rows.anchor: The real thing is a person’s intent.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reflection on human creation and the system sustaining people establishes God’s providence, power, wisdom, oneness, resurrection, and certain recompense.
rows.anchor: attention is now drawn to the creation of man and to the tremendous system set up by God to nurture and sustain him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One who formed a person from clay and a drop of water can recreate him, and creation’s care implies accountability for how human qualities are used.
rows.anchor: How can it be difficult for the Creator Who has created man in such a grand mould from clay and a drop of water to recreate him?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beasts are providential resources deliberately suited to human needs, including transport, milk, meat, wool, and hides; these benefits call for gratitude.
rows.anchor: If man needed milk, meat, wool and hides, God created different beasts to provide him with these needs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The elaborate provision of blessings entails a day when God rewards those who honour them and punishes the ungrateful.
rows.anchor: those who fulfilled their rights be rewarded and those who forgot God after receiving them be punished for their ingratitude.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revival of the earth by rain makes it no difficulty for the same God to recreate the world after its death.
rows.anchor: every season to recreate this world after it dies?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yaqīnūn expresses intention: signs do not benefit people unless they intend to accept them, and the unwilling invent doubts.
rows.anchor: unless people have the intention to accept them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtilāf means the successive alternation of night and day, whose temperamental differences are essential to the universe’s existence and sustenance.
rows.anchor: difference in the temperament of the night and the day which is essential for the existence, sustenance and well-being of this universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rizq here denotes water, using the effect to signify its cause, a usage common across languages.
rows.anchor: Here the effect connotes the cause.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day have opposing qualities yet form a harmonious pair for human nurture, proving they share one Creator; separate gods could not sustain life in such harmony.
rows.anchor: to nurture man both of them form a harmonious pair.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain from heaven revives the earth, including apparently lifeless land, showing that a single will governs heaven and earth and preparing the analogy of recreation.
rows.anchor: there is not a single place in it in which any form of life can be seen when suddenly it springs to life after receiving rain.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Winds display God’s power, mercy, providence, and punishment; one controller can make them a boon or bane, as in Moses’ rescue and Pharaoh’s destruction.
rows.anchor: It was because of this movement of the wind that God saved Moses (sws) and his people and destroyed the Pharaoh and his people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farmers and sailors depend on suitable winds, and providence exposes human claims to control them; one Being rules the elements, down to the movement of a leaf.
rows.anchor: Without His permission, even a single leaf cannot move from its place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cosmic signs benefit those who use their intellect; people who use reason only for material gain miss their deeper meaning.
rows.anchor: only those will benefit from them who use their intellect.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding three verses show signs of monotheism and the Hereafter everywhere; those willing to reason can acknowledge them, while chosen blindness persists despite their clarity.
rows.anchor: For the others too, these signs are not concealed on the condition that they have the courage to acknowledge and fully accept

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse assures the Prophet and rebukes his adversaries; its demonstrative refers to the inner and outer signs just described.
rows.anchor: This verse sounds an assurance to the Prophet (sws) and rebukes his adversaries.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs disclose God’s oneness, power, wisdom, and the day of recompense; the Qur’ān recites their full implications, so rejecting this evident case leaves no better proof to accept.
rows.anchor: So evident are these signs that no sensible person can deny them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bi-l-ḥaqq denotes the certain, factual consequences reached by reflecting on the signs.
rows.anchor: refers to the certain and factual consequences which one reaches after reflecting on these signs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specialists examine limited mechanisms—such as weather or anatomy—but overlook the reality of the Controller and His rights, even when their observations are accurate.
rows.anchor: their observation and analysis is confined to the nature of wind movement and its effects.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān’s call rests on arguments in the world within and around people and on reason and human nature, rather than coercion.
rows.anchor: arguments found in the world within man and that around him as well as on the obvious norms of sense and human nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God and His signs are self-evident; denial reflects enslavement to desires and material things, so demands for new miracles deserve no attention.
rows.anchor: they are mere slaves of their desires and worship material things.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rebuke continues: destruction awaits those who deny the signs to justify their sinful lives.
rows.anchor: Destruction awaits these people who have denied all these signs only to give credence to their sinful lives.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kadhdhāb describes one who distorts the signs’ reality through desire; foremost are Quraysh idolaters who disfigured Abraham’s religion, though the charge applies generally.
rows.anchor: The foremost people on whom this verse applies are the idolaters of the Quraysh who had distorted and disfigured the religion of Abraham (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Athīm means a sinner, especially one who neglects obligations to God and the rights of others; the pairing links distortion with evading duties and persisting in sin.
rows.anchor: neither discharges his obligations nor fulfils the rights of others.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders arrogantly turned away from the Prophet’s recitation as if they had heard nothing, even avoiding his gatherings or repulsively leaving them.
rows.anchor: they very arrogantly walk away as if they heard nothing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not hearing a message might excuse someone, but the Prophet personally went to them and vehemently delivered God’s message.
rows.anchor: if God’s message has not reached someone and he remains unaware of it, then he may be afforded with a legitimate excuse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the previous verse’s direct recitation by the Prophet, this verse treats people who learn a Qur’ānic verse or directive through someone else and ridicule it to prevent others being influenced.
rows.anchor: when they would hear a Qur’ ānic verse or directive through someone else

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Leaders could not answer listeners’ interest with rational objections, so they mocked the Qur’ān; the tactic might temporarily deceive the weak and is used by devils in every age.
rows.anchor: could not convince them through arguments by saying that such and such a verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their haughtiness before truth results in humiliation in the Hereafter; torment accompanied by humiliation is reserved for the arrogant.
rows.anchor: His greatest torment is one which is accompanied by humiliation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waraʾ can mean back or front according to context; here Hell is ahead of the rejecters.
rows.anchor: It can mean both “the back” and “the front”.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their illegally acquired wealth and the deities or intercessors they served besides God cannot help them in Hell.
rows.anchor: will their illegally acquired treasures and riches which was the reason of their arrogance and evasion from the truth be of any avail to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised punishment is grievous and beyond what people can imagine now.
rows.anchor: its horrible nature cannot be imagined today.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’ān is guidance from God, not a joke; those who deny or ridicule its verses face a painful torment.
rows.anchor: Those who deny its verses or make fun of them should remember that they will face a painful torment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rajz describes a torment that produces shivers and makes hearts tremble.
rows.anchor: which will cause the hearts to shiver and tremble.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four intervening verses warn Quraysh and reassure the Prophet before the discourse resumes its argument for monotheism and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The previous four verses were interposed between the arguments cited in support of monotheism and the Hereafter so that the leaders of the Quraysh are warned forthwith and the Prophet (sws) is assured.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the sea serve people, and its ships sail by His directive; this is a God-established arrangement rather than an independent force.
rows.anchor: Had God not directed so, a ship would have drowned in the sea the way smaller objects are drowned when they enter it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A purpose meaning travel is suppressed before the phrase about seeking bounty; the conjunction wāw signals it, and trade seeks God’s blessings.
rows.anchor: The particle of conjunction وis an evidence to this suppression.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The response to God’s providence is gratitude, which forms the foundation of worship; Islahi discusses this in al-Fātiḥah.
rows.anchor: It should be kept in mind that it is this feeling of gratitude which is the foundation of worshipping God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage first highlights the sea because it is a powerful, apparently uncontrollable feature familiar through human experience.
rows.anchor: the sea is the most powerful of things that comes in the observation of man and which is apparently uncontrollable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamīʿan grammatically relates to minhu, not to the preceding words.
rows.anchor: does not relate to the previous words; it relates to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the sea, the discussion turns to all the other things of the heavens and earth that God has placed in human service.
rows.anchor: the same God has put all other things of the heavens and the earth in the service of man.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After naming the sea, the passage generalizes to all things in heaven and earth, since the sea is a powerful and familiar example of what appears uncontrollable.
rows.anchor: After this specific mention, a reference is made to the general things of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jamīʿan minhu means all these things serve people directly or indirectly; God alone harnessed them, since He created and controls them.
rows.anchor: all these, in fact, have been harnessed by God because He alone is their Creator and He alone controls them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nature’s elements cannot be gods because they are subservient; though conflicting, they harmonize like machine parts, showing one governing will.
rows.anchor: This congruence between them shows that a single will prevails in this universe.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Providence, mercy, and wisdom require a day of recompense; otherwise God would be powerless, insensitive, or merely entertaining Himself, contrary to His attributes.
rows.anchor: His knowledge, mercy and wisdom necessitate that He also bring about a day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arguments for monotheism and the Hereafter abound, but reflection is required and God does not force people to undertake it.
rows.anchor: The only thing that is lacking is reflection and deliberation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ṣafḥ means to forgive and overlook someone.
rows.anchor: The word O here means to forgive and ignore someone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person who treats desire as master disregards explicit divine directives and follows desires and religious innovations, as Islahi discusses regarding Jews in al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: such a person is not a slave of God; he is the slave of his desires and religious innovations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews’ deprivation was not lack of faith’s light but failure to value divinely given knowledge; after receiving clear injunctions, their stubborn dispute led God to let them stray, as in 45:17.
rows.anchor: instead of giving due importance to the knowledge given to them by God, they only followed their desires and religious innovations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi connects God’s sealing of hearts to the discussion of the Jews in al-Baqarah 2:7 and says the Qur’ān mentions Jews with this attribute.
rows.anchor: nature of God setting seal on the hearts of people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A governing noun is suppressed after min, understood as asking who can guide people whose hearts God has sealed according to His established practice.
rows.anchor: The implication is that who can guide people on whose hearts a seal has been set as per the established practice of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should not be surprised that literate claimants to scripture oppose the Qur’ān and befriend idolaters: God guides those who value guidance and can lead others astray through it, as 2:26 says.
rows.anchor: God guides only those who duly value His guidance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next section addresses rejecters’ demand to have their forefathers raised as proof of the Resurrection and begins to refute it by portraying their inevitable fate.
rows.anchor: when they were warned of it, they would say that if it is to come, then the Prophet (sws) should raise their forefathers back to life!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section shows that no deity or intercessor can save rejecters from God’s punishment; triumph belongs to those who believe in monotheism and the Hereafter and rely on their pious deeds.
rows.anchor: no deity or intercessor will be able to save them from the punishment of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The succeeding verses portray the fate of the rejecters and the triumph of believers rather than treating their demand as evidence against resurrection.
rows.anchor: the supreme triumph will be achieved only by those who profess faith in the Hereafter and in monotheism
